Translations are plain JSON files: one root file per locale for shared keys, and one file per page and locale for that page's keys. Read this when you add pages, share keys between them or set up fallbacks. You learn which file a key must go in, what a page can see, and when each file is loaded.

locales/
├── en.json                 # root: menus, footer, buttons
├── de.json
└── pages/
    ├── index/              # pages/index.vue
    │   ├── en.json
    │   └── de.json
    ├── about/              # pages/about.vue
    │   ├── en.json
    │   └── de.json
    └── products-id/        # pages/products/[id].vue
        ├── en.json
        └── de.json

A page's dictionary is its root file merged with its page file, deeply (every level). The page file wins on a clash:
language-json shiki shiki-themes material-theme-lighter material-theme material-theme-palenight
language-ts shiki shiki-themes material-theme-lighter material-theme material-theme-palenight
A page without its own folder gets the root dictionary alone. Keys of other pages are not visible.
A key missing in the active locale is taken from its fallback locale before the key itself is shown:
is the weakest layer, under every chain.
Each locale in the chain adds its root file, then its page file, from the weakest fallback up to the active locale. So the active locale's root file beats a fallback locale's page file.

How a page loads its dictionary
Locale JSON files are built into a payload tree, stored in public/ on Node or in server assets on Edge, read by a server loader, then used by $t on the server and fetched for $t in the browser
The module builds one payload per page and locale:
Nitro detects the locale and the page loads its payload from the server loader directly, with no HTTP request. The dictionary is not written into the HTML payload, so pages stay small.
The browser fetches the same payload. The server already emitted a
for it, so the fetch starts with the HTML.
The next page's payload replaces the dictionary. The leaving page's keys still resolve until it is gone (end of the page transition, or

), so a fading-out page does not flash raw keys. A chunk that fails to load (network error, 4xx or 5xx, a body that is not an object) leaves the current dictionary in place, and the next navigation loads it again. A failed locale switch is the same:
